strengths: Provides a rigorous, exact geometric characterization (feasible PPV/FOR region, star-convexity, piecewise hyperbolic boundary) of classifiers attainable from a group-calibrated score, extending prior work (Baumann et al., 2022) that required continuity and full-support assumptions to the practically relevant finite-valued score setting.

Derives a clean and efficient post-processing algorithm (boundary tracing via the fractional-knapsack-style greedy rule) that computes the optimal sufficiency-constrained classifier for a broad class of loss functions, with explicit closed-form reduction to solving quadratics.

Extends the analysis to a second, practically important objective—minimizing deviation from separation subject to sufficiency—showing it can be optimized within the same geometric/algorithmic framework, which nicely bridges two fairness notions known to be generally incompatible.

The paper is well organized theoretically, connects clearly to established fairness literature (Chouldechova, Kleinberg et al., Hardt et al., Canetti et al., Baumann et al., Benger & Ligett), and includes detailed proofs for essentially all claims in the appendix.
The COMPAS case study offers a concrete, interpretable illustration of the method, showing group-specific threshold behavior and near-optimal accuracy relative to the unconstrained optimum.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is minimal: only a single dataset (COMPAS) and a single illustrative run are reported, without comparison to alternative approaches for achieving sufficiency (e.g., Canetti et al.'s abstention-based method or Baumann et al.'s post-processing), and without any assessment of variability/robustness across data splits or datasets.

The entire framework assumes the population distribution P(Y,S,A) (and thus perfect group-calibration) is known exactly; finite-sample estimation error in calibration curves and score distributions is not analyzed, even though the COMPAS experiment relies on empirically estimated calibration curves from a data split, which could materially affect the correctness/robustness of the derived optimal classifier in practice.

The method may require randomized decisions at breakpoints, which raises practical and ethical considerations (e.g., transparency, reproducibility, and acceptability of randomized decisions in high-stakes settings such as bail) that are not discussed.

The main text focuses exclusively on the binary-group case; while the authors state the extension to multiple groups is straightforward, this is not demonstrated, and the combinatorial complexity of tracing pairwise boundaries for more than two groups is left unaddressed.

Limited discussion of how sensitive the practical usefulness of the approach is to violations of the group-calibration assumption (the paper notes COMPAS scores are not properly calibrated and relies on an ad hoc recalibration procedure, but does not quantify how deviations from true calibration affect the guarantees).

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: achieving optimal classification under the sufficiency (predictive parity) fairness criterion when scores are finite-valued/discrete, relaxing the continuity and full-support assumptions made in prior work (Baumann et al., 2022).

The geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region is elegant: star-convexity around (pi, pi), the piecewise-hyperbolic boundary structure, and its connection to fractional-knapsack-style greedy thresholding are nicely derived and proven rigorously in the appendices.

The reduction of both loss minimization and deviation-from-separation minimization to tracing a common boundary curve (Algorithm 1) is a unifying and practically useful algorithmic contribution, with closed-form quadratic sub-problems on each piece.
The derivations are careful, with detailed step-by-step proofs provided in the appendix for essentially every claim, which aids verifiability.

The connection drawn between sufficiency-optimal classifiers and deviation from separation is a natural and interesting extension that could be useful for practitioners weighing different fairness objectives.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is extremely limited: a single real dataset (COMPAS) with one scalar accuracy comparison (0.677 vs 0.681) and no comparison to existing baselines (e.g., Canetti et al.'s abstention-based classifiers or Baumann et al.'s utility-maximizing post-processing), making it hard to judge the practical benefit of the proposed method over alternatives.

There is no empirical or theoretical treatment of estimation error: the entire framework assumes the joint distribution P(Y,S,A) (and group-calibration of S) is known exactly, but in practice scores and calibration curves must be estimated from finite data. The COMPAS experiment performs a single train/calibration split without reporting variability across splits or sensitivity to calibration error, which is a serious reproducibility/robustness gap given that the paper's central claims rely on exact calibration.

No synthetic experiments are provided to illustrate algorithmic behavior under controlled conditions (e.g., varying group base-rate gaps, varying support sizes, varying degree of miscalibration), which would help validate the theory beyond a single anecdotal case study and demonstrate how far performance degrades with realistic calibration violations.
No runtime/complexity analysis or empirical demonstration of scalability of Algorithm 1, despite it being presented as a key practical contribution.

The extension to more than two groups is claimed to be 'straightforward' but is never worked out, even though the intersection-of-feasible-regions argument central to the method seems likely to become substantially more complex (intersection of more than two nondecreasing curves, more intervals/breakpoints) -- this understates a potentially significant limitation.

The overall technical contribution, while rigorous, is relatively incremental relative to Baumann et al. (2022): it generalizes the continuous-score result to the discrete-score case primarily via careful bookkeeping of breakpoints/intervals, rather than introducing fundamentally new conceptual tools; the significance of this generalization for practical fairness pipelines is not strongly demonstrated given the thin empirical section.

The paper does not discuss robustness of the sufficiency-optimal classifier to misspecification of group membership A or to intersectional/multiple protected attributes, which are common concerns in real deployments.

Figures such as Figure 2 are illustrative schematics rather than grounded in real or realistic data, and the single real-data figure (Figure 3) is not accompanied by confidence intervals or multiple-seed analysis, limiting confidence in the practical conclusions drawn from it.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: prior post-processing solutions for sufficiency (e.g., Baumann et al., 2022) assume continuous, full-support score distributions, while this paper handles the practically common case of finite-valued, group-calibrated scores (e.g., COMPAS deciles).

The geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region is elegant and rigorously derived, with the star-convexity property and piecewise hyperbolic boundary structure (Theorems 3.3-3.4) providing real insight into the structure of sufficiency-constrained classifiers.

The reduction of the loss-minimization and deviation-from-separation minimization problems to tracing the boundary of the intersection of subgroup-feasible regions is a clean algorithmic contribution, and the paper shows that both objectives reduce to solving quadratics on each piece, making the method computationally tractable (Algorithms 1-2).

The extension to minimizing deviation from separation under a sufficiency constraint is a nice additional contribution that reuses the same geometric machinery, addressing the known incompatibility between sufficiency and separation in a constructive way.

Proofs appear complete and carefully worked out in the appendices, and the paper is transparent about assumptions (finite support, group-calibration, binary A, nonconstant classifiers) and about degenerate cases (Appendix D).

The COMPAS illustration is a useful, recognizable example that concretely demonstrates the necessity of group-specific thresholds under sufficiency and shows the method can be applied with estimated calibration curves.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is minimal: a single dataset (COMPAS) and a single illustrative example are used to support the claim that the deviation-from-separation-minimizing classifier is 'often' comparable in performance to the loss-optimal one; this general claim is not well substantiated beyond one instance where the two actually coincide.

The method's optimality guarantees rely on the strong assumption of exact group-calibration (or known P(Y,S,A)); in practice, scores are rarely perfectly calibrated, and the paper does not analyze sensitivity/robustness of the resulting classifiers to calibration or estimation error, despite using empirically estimated calibration curves in the case study.

The extension to more than two groups is asserted as 'straightforward' but not actually derived or demonstrated, leaving an important practical generalization unaddressed and unverified (the quadratic-root-based algorithm may not trivially extend when more than two feasible regions must be intersected simultaneously).

The paper offers no comparison, empirical or theoretical, against the two main competing approaches it cites (Canetti et al., 2019 abstention-based method; Baumann et al., 2022 continuous-score method) to contextualize the practical benefit of the proposed exact finite-score solution.

Significance is somewhat narrow: the contribution is a specific geometric/optimization result for a single fairness criterion (sufficiency) under an idealized assumption (group-calibrated finite scores), which, while rigorous, may have limited reach without broader empirical demonstration across more realistic or large-scale decision-making settings.

Presentation is dense and heavy with notation (feasible sets, boundary intervals, breakpoints, multiple theorems indexed by k, l, i), which, combined with minimal empirical grounding until Section 7, may make the paper's practical implications harder to access for a broader ICML audience.

strengths: Provides a rigorous, exact geometric characterization (star-convexity, piecewise hyperbolic boundary structure) of the feasible PPV/FOR region for binary classifiers built on calibrated scores, which is a genuinely novel and elegant analytical tool.

Extends prior work (Baumann et al., 2022) that assumed continuous, full-support score distributions to the practically important finite-valued score setting, which matches real systems like COMPAS and FICO that use discrete score bins.

Derives a concrete, efficient post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that traces the boundary of the intersection of group-wise feasible regions and can optimize a wide class of objectives, including 0-1 loss and a deviation-from-separation measure, unifying two seemingly separate fairness problems within one framework.

Includes a formal robustness analysis bounding predictive-parity violation by twice the maximum calibration error when scores are only approximately group-calibrated, with both synthetic and real (ACS Income) empirical support, which strengthens practical applicability.

Empirical illustrations span three different real/semi-real datasets (FICO, COMPAS, ACS Income) with an end-to-end pipeline (including model training and calibration) for the ACS case, giving a reasonably complete picture of the method's applicability and reproducibility.

The observation and proof that classifiers minimizing deviation from separation can be found via the same boundary-tracing algorithm and often achieve near-optimal accuracy is a useful and non-obvious practical takeaway.
weaknesses: The framework and detailed algorithm are developed only for the binary-group case; extension to more than two protected groups is deferred entirely to future work, even though the conclusion acknowledges this is a significant practical limitation (feasibility becomes increasingly restrictive with more groups).

The method's central assumption of access to (exactly or approximately) group-calibrated finite-valued scores is fairly strong; in the COMPAS experiment, calibration is not verified but essentially constructed synthetically by assigning pooled empirical outcome rates to decile scores, which weakens the realism of that case study.

There is no empirical comparison against existing post-processing baselines for sufficiency/predictive parity (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022's continuous-score approach adapted to discretized data, or Zeng et al. 2022), making it hard to gauge practical advantages beyond the theoretical guarantees.

The deviation-from-separation analysis is tied to one specific total-variation-based measure (Benger & Ligett, 2025); it is unclear how sensitive the resulting optimal classifier and its favorable comparison to the loss-optimal one are to the choice of separation-deviation metric.

The presentation is very notation-heavy and mathematically dense (extensive appendices with many auxiliary lemmas), which may limit accessibility to a broader ICML audience despite the work's technical soundness.

The practical significance of exact sufficiency in real deployments is not deeply discussed—since exact predictive parity is a stringent binary-decision fairness notion, and the paper does not discuss when practitioners would prefer this exact approach over approximate or relaxed alternatives beyond a brief mention in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper identifies and rigorously formalizes an important and under-appreciated gap in the fairness literature: unlike independence and separation, sufficiency is not preserved by thresholding group-calibrated scores, even when scores equal the true conditional probabilities. This motivation is well-argued and grounded in prior literature (Chouldechova 2017, Canetti et al. 2019, Baumann et al. 2022).

The core theoretical contribution—a geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region attainable by a classifier based on a finite-valued calibrated score, including star-convexity around (π, π) and a piecewise-hyperbolic boundary traced by a greedy/knapsack-type soft-thresholding rule (Theorem 3.3)—is elegant, non-trivial, and appears mathematically sound; the appendix supplies full, careful proofs.

The extension to two groups via intersection of feasible regions, together with Algorithm 1 for tracing the boundary of the intersection and optimizing an arbitrary objective (loss or deviation from separation) piecewise via quadratics, is a genuinely useful and reasonably efficient algorithmic contribution that goes beyond the continuous/full-support assumptions of Baumann et al. (2022), addressing a practically relevant discrete-score setting.

The paper also derives the optimal classifier minimizing a total-variation-based deviation-from-separation measure (Benger & Ligett, 2025) subject to exact sufficiency, showing it is obtainable with the same machinery — a nice, low-cost secondary contribution connecting two fairness notions.

Empirical illustrations span three settings (FICO aggregate statistics, COMPAS, and an end-to-end ACS Income pipeline with real model training/calibration), and the paper includes a thoughtful robustness analysis (Appendix J) bounding predictive-parity violation by 2ε under approximate group-calibration, with supporting synthetic and real-data experiments showing the bound is conservative in practice.
weaknesses: The framework is restricted to binary protected groups throughout the main development; the multi-group case is explicitly deferred to future work in the conclusion, which meaningfully limits real-world applicability since many fairness applications involve more than two groups (e.g., intersectional attributes).

The central assumption of exact (or near-exact) group-calibration is strong; while the robustness analysis is a good-faith attempt to address this, the core theory and 'exact optimality' claims apply only under exact calibration, and practical calibration (as in the ACS Income experiment) is only approximate, so the 'optimal' guarantees are somewhat idealized relative to deployment settings.

The empirical evaluation is largely illustrative rather than comparative: there is no direct empirical benchmarking against the two main prior approaches discussed in Section 1 (Canetti et al. 2019's abstention-based method, Baumann et al. 2022's utility-maximization under sufficiency), so it is hard to gauge the practical advantage of the proposed exact method over existing alternatives in terms of accuracy/utility trade-offs.

The COMPAS experiment constructs 'group-calibrated' scores by assigning each decile score its pooled (group-agnostic) empirical outcome rate, which is an approximation of convenience rather than a genuine group-calibrated score; treating this as if it were exactly the assumed setting somewhat weakens the empirical validity of this case study.

The scope of the contribution is fairly narrow and specialized (binary decisions, binary groups, finite/discretized scores, a single fairness criterion at a time), and the paper does not deeply explore how the accuracy cost of exact sufficiency compares with other established fairness-accuracy trade-off curves (e.g., under separation or independence constraints), limiting the broader significance of the results.

Presentation is dense and heavily deferred to appendices (nearly all proofs, several derivations, and even key formulas for the algorithm's inner workings), which, combined with substantial notational overhead (many indexed quantities such as pk, qk, ck, Jk,l,i, Φk,l), makes the paper hard to read and reduces accessibility for readers primarily interested in applying the method.
Code is only promised ('will be made available') rather than currently provided, which limits immediate reproducibility verification.

strengths: The paper closes an important gap identified in prior literature: existing exact-sufficiency post-processing methods (e.g., Baumann et al., 2022) rely on continuity/full-support assumptions that fail for the practically common case of discrete, finite-valued scores (e.g., COMPAS deciles, credit-score bins). This work gives an exact treatment for that setting.

The core theoretical contribution is elegant and non-trivial: the star-convexity of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region, the reduction of boundary-tracing to a fractional-knapsack/greedy threshold argument (Theorem 3.3), and the resulting piecewise-hyperbolic characterization of the boundary (Theorem 3.4) are clean, well-proved results with clear geometric intuition (Figure 1).

The framework is general enough to optimize multiple objectives on the same feasible-region boundary (arbitrary loss functions via Section 5, and deviation from separation via Section 6), unifying two practically relevant fairness/accuracy trade-off questions under one algorithmic machinery (Algorithm 1).

The paper directly addresses estimation robustness: Appendix J proves a linear bound on predictive-parity violation as a function of calibration error and empirically validates that observed violations are typically well below this worst-case bound, both in a synthetic setting and on ACS Income.

Three complementary real-data illustrations (FICO, COMPAS, ACS Income) show the method end-to-end, including a full pipeline with model training, cross-fitted calibration, and post-processing on held-out data, and quantify the accuracy/fairness trade-off concretely (e.g., 0.8819 vs. 0.8676 accuracy on FICO).

The relationship between the loss-optimal and separation-deviation-minimizing solutions is explored, showing they often nearly coincide empirically, which is a useful practical takeaway for practitioners choosing between objectives.
weaknesses: The central assumption of (exact) group-calibration is strong, and the COMPAS experiment does not actually use group-calibrated scores from a real predictor — it constructs a synthetic 'group-calibrated' score by pooling the empirical outcome rate per decile across groups, which is a significant deviation from a realistic use case and somewhat undercuts the illustrative value of that case study.

The method is developed only for binary protected attribute A; extension to more than two groups is left as future work, and the paper itself notes (Section 8) that exact feasibility becomes increasingly restrictive as the number of groups grows, which limits applicability to many real-world settings with multi-category protected attributes.

The empirical evaluation, while illustrative, is relatively narrow: aside from ACS Income, results are largely single-run point estimates without uncertainty quantification, and there is no direct empirical comparison against the abstention-based (Canetti et al., 2019) or continuous-score (Baumann et al., 2022) baselines discussed in related work, making it hard to gauge practical advantages/disadvantages quantitatively.

The paper requires access to group membership A at decision time to compute the post-processed classifier, which raises potential disparate-treatment/legal concerns in some jurisdictions; this practical/ethical consideration is not discussed.

The presentation is very notation-heavy and much of the technical substance (all main proofs, the active-boundary quadratic characterization, loss/∆sep minimization derivations) is deferred to a lengthy appendix, making the main text somewhat dense and less self-contained for readers who want to verify claims without consulting ~15 pages of appendix.
